label: Cubics and the Group Law
notes: Open the chapter. Smooth plane cubics carry one of the most beautiful structures in mathematics: an abelian group on their points. The deck follows printed pages 35 through 54 and develops the Weierstrass form, the chord-and-tangent construction, the proof that addition is associative, and the consequences that make cubics utterly different from conics.

label: Smooth Plane Cubics
notes: Introduce the nonsingular plane cubic and its Weierstrass normal form, obtained by projective coordinate changes. Unlike a conic, a smooth cubic is not rational: it cannot be parametrized by the line. This failure of rationality is the first sign that cubics have genuinely richer geometry and demands a new organizing idea, the group law.

label: The Chord-and-Tangent Law
notes: Define addition geometrically. A line meets the cubic in three points by Bezout, and the chord-and-tangent rule turns this into a binary operation: collinear points sum to a fixed identity. Tangent lines handle doubling. The construction is entirely geometric, yet it produces a well-defined commutative operation on the points of the curve.

label: Associativity
notes: Address the one hard axiom. Commutativity and inverses are easy, but associativity is not obvious from the construction. Prove it using the fact that two cubics through eight common points share the ninth, a consequence of counting intersections. This synthetic argument is the conceptual heart of the chapter and the deepest point in this part.

label: Consequences
notes: Explore what the group buys us. Over the rationals the points form a finitely generated abelian group by the Mordell theorem, the source of deep arithmetic. Torsion points and flexes appear as special elements. The same curves underpin modern elliptic-curve cryptography, showing how this classical geometry reaches into computation.

label: Recap
notes: Close the chapter. Smooth cubics admit a Weierstrass form, are not rational, and carry an abelian group defined by chords and tangents, with associativity following from the nine-point property. The group law makes cubics the gateway to elliptic curves, and Part II now turns to the general theory of affine varieties.
